cards.front: At every feeding step in a food chain, by which three routes ('doors') can energy leave?
cards.back: Passed up as consumer production, dropped into detritus (uneaten, or as feces), or lost as heat.
cards.quote: At every feeding step, energy leaves by one of three doors: passed up as consumer production, dropped into detritus (uneaten, or as feces), or lost as heat.

cards.front: Why does production shrink fast as you move up a food chain?
cards.back: The share passed up at each step is a product of three fractions: consumption × assimilation × net production efficiency. Multiplying several fractions below 1 gives a small number, and the losses compound step after step.
cards.quote: The share passed up is a product of three fractions, consumption × assimilation × net production efficiency, so production shrinks fast up a food chain.

cards.front: Does energy cycle through an ecosystem the way matter does?
cards.back: No. Energy never returns to the producers: it is stored for a while or leaves as heat. Only matter cycles.
cards.quote: Energy never returns to the producers: it is stored for a while or leaves as heat.

cards.front: Production is the {{c1::rate}} at which new organic matter, or its energy, is formed per unit area or volume per unit time.
cards.back: For example kJ m^-2 yr^-1 or g C m^-2 yr^-1. Biomass (standing crop) is a stock, with no time unit.
cards.quote: Production is the rate at which new organic matter, or its energy, is formed per unit area or volume per unit time
cards.section: Production is a rate: GPP, NPP and NEP

cards.front: In a lake, the phytoplankton standing crop is smaller than the zooplankton standing crop that feeds on it. How can a small producer stock support a larger consumer stock?
cards.back: Through fast turnover. Biomass is a stock and production is a rate; fast-dividing phytoplankton can produce a lot per unit time while little is standing at any moment.
cards.quote: A small stock can sit on a large production if it turns over quickly, as fast-dividing phytoplankton do.
cards.section: Production is a rate: GPP, NPP and NEP

cards.front: How is net primary production (NPP) related to gross primary production (GPP)?
cards.back: NPP = GPP − Ra, where Ra is the autotrophic respiration of the producers themselves. Real plants often respire roughly half of the energy they fix.
cards.quote: Real plants often respire roughly half of the energy they fix.
cards.section: Production is a rate: GPP, NPP and NEP

cards.front: Net ecosystem production (NEP) subtracts {{c1::Reco}}, the respiration of the whole ecosystem: Ra plus the respiration of animals, fungi and bacteria.
cards.back: NEP = GPP − Reco.
cards.quote: Net ecosystem production (NEP) subtracts Reco, the respiration of the whole ecosystem: Ra plus the respiration of animals, fungi and bacteria.
cards.section: Production is a rate: GPP, NPP and NEP

cards.front: An illustrative closed ecosystem (no organic matter carried in or out) has GPP = 8,000 kJ m^-2 yr^-1. Producers respire 4,400; animals, fungi and bacteria respire 2,600. Find NPP, Reco and NEP.
cards.quote: it is what the ecosystem stores, and GPP = Reco + NEP: everything fixed is either respired or stored.
cards.section: Production is a rate: GPP, NPP and NEP

cards.front: Why is gross primary production (GPP) at ecosystem scale always an estimate?
cards.back: No method observes GPP directly at ecosystem scale. Each method measures one door, or the net, and infers the rest, so GPP comes with a method attached.
cards.quote: No method observes GPP directly at ecosystem scale; each measures one door, or the net, and infers the rest.
cards.section: Measuring it: bottles, harvests and towers

cards.front: In a light-and-dark-bottle experiment, what does the change in oxygen in the light bottle measure?
cards.back: Net community production = (L − O_start) / t: photosynthetic gain minus respiratory loss.
cards.quote: The light bottle gains oxygen from photosynthesis and loses it to respiration, so its change is net community production = (L − O_start) / t.
cards.section: Measuring it: bottles, harvests and towers

cards.front: In a light-and-dark-bottle experiment, what does the oxygen loss in the dark bottle measure?
cards.back: Respiration of the whole community in the bottle = (O_start − D) / t, because the dark bottle only respires.
cards.quote: The dark bottle only respires, so its loss is respiration = (O_start − D) / t.
cards.section: Measuring it: bottles, harvests and towers

cards.front: Why does gross production from light and dark bottles reduce to (L − D) / t, with no need for the starting oxygen?
cards.back: GPP = net community production + respiration = (L − O_start)/t + (O_start − D)/t. O_start appears once with a minus and once with a plus, so it cancels.
cards.quote: The starting value O_start appears once with a minus and once with a plus, so it drops out.
cards.section: Measuring it: bottles, harvests and towers

cards.front: Paired light and dark bottles of sea water start at 9.0 mg O2/L. After 3 hours the light bottle reads 10.5 and the dark bottle 8.4. Find net community production, respiration and GPP per hour.
cards.why: Assumes equal respiration in light and dark and no gas escape.
cards.quote: This assumes equal respiration in light and dark and no gas escape.
cards.section: Measuring it: bottles, harvests and towers

cards.front: Why is the net from a light bottle of lake water not phytoplankton net primary production?
cards.back: The bottle also holds bacteria and zooplankton, so its net is community production. It is also in oxygen units until a justified conversion to carbon is made.
cards.quote: The bottle also holds bacteria and zooplankton, so its net is community production, not phytoplankton NPP, in oxygen units until a stated conversion to carbon is justified.
cards.section: Measuring it: bottles, harvests and towers

cards.front: In a light-and-dark-bottle study, suppose the community actually respires faster in the light than in the dark. Is the calculated GPP too high or too low, and why?
cards.back: Too low. GPP is estimated as net community production plus dark-bottle respiration; if respiration in the light is larger, the true photosynthesis is net production plus that larger loss.
cards.why: The method assumes respiration is equal in light and dark.
cards.quote: respiration is assumed equal in light and dark (in the light it can differ) and the bottle sealed.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: What does clipping and weighing grassland plants at the season's peak estimate, and how good is the estimate?
cards.back: Aboveground NPP, as a rough and usually low estimate.
cards.quote: In grassland, clipping and weighing the plants at the season's peak gives a rough, usually low estimate of aboveground NPP.
cards.section: Measuring it: bottles, harvests and towers

cards.front: In nine forest stands in Korea, NPP was estimated by summing woody growth, litterfall and fine-root growth. What did the fine-root share show?
cards.back: Fine roots made up 18 to 44% of estimated NPP, so a forest estimate that leaves out belowground growth can miss a large part of production.
cards.quote: Gwangneung Experimental Forest, Korea, where fine roots made up 18 to 44% of the estimated NPP.
cards.section: Measuring it: bottles, harvests and towers

cards.front: What does an eddy-covariance flux tower measure directly, and how are GPP and ecosystem respiration obtained from it?
cards.back: Only net ecosystem exchange (NEE). A partitioning model splits it, commonly by fitting respiration to night-time data and extrapolating it into the day.
cards.quote: The tower sees only this net; a partitioning model splits it into GPP and Reco, commonly by fitting respiration to night-time data (no photosynthesis) and extrapolating it into the day.
cards.section: Measuring it: bottles, harvests and towers

cards.front: A tower counts release to the air as positive. Over a year, a forest's GPP is 1,500 and Reco is 1,700 g C m^-2 yr^-1. What is its NEE, and is it a carbon sink or source?
cards.back: NEE = Reco − GPP = 1,700 − 1,500 = +200 g C m^-2 yr^-1: a net source. NEP is −200, the mirror image.
cards.quote: With release counted as positive, NEE = Reco − GPP, the mirror image of NEP, so an ecosystem that takes up carbon has a negative NEE.
cards.section: Measuring it: bottles, harvests and towers

cards.front: At a Scots pine forest in Finland, GPP estimated by two carbonyl sulfide methods averaged 7% and 23% above the CO2-based estimate. What does this show?
cards.back: Partitioning methods disagree at the same site, so GPP is an estimate with a method attached, and agreement among methods is not independent validation.
cards.quote: daily GPP estimates from two methods based on carbonyl sulfide, a gas leaves take up along with CO2, averaged 7% and 23% above the CO2-based estimate.
cards.section: Splitting a tower's net flux

cards.front: Of what an animal ingests (eats, I), part leaves as feces (egestion); the rest is {{c1::assimilated}} (A), absorbed into the body.
cards.back: A = I − egestion; P = A − R.
cards.quote: what it assimilates, A
cards.section: Following energy through a consumer

cards.front: Give the ratios for consumption efficiency, assimilation efficiency and net production efficiency.
cards.back: Consumption efficiency = I / P below (production of the level eaten). Assimilation efficiency = A / I. Net production efficiency = P / A.
cards.quote: consumption efficiency, I / P below (P below is the production of the level eaten); assimilation efficiency, A / I; and net production efficiency, P / A.
cards.section: Following energy through a consumer

cards.front: What is trophic transfer efficiency (TTE)?
cards.back: Production at one level over production at the level below, in matched units and time. It equals consumption × assimilation × net production efficiency.
cards.quote: Their product is the trophic transfer efficiency (TTE): production at one level over production at the level below, in matched units and time.
cards.section: Following energy through a consumer

cards.front: Why does consumption × assimilation × net production efficiency equal P / P below?
cards.back: (I / P below) × (A / I) × (P / A): the I terms cancel and the A terms cancel, leaving P / P below.
cards.quote: Multiply the three fractions: I on top of the second cancels I on the bottom of the first, and A on top of the third cancels A on the bottom of the second.
cards.section: Following energy through a consumer

cards.front: Why does assimilation efficiency tend to be higher for carnivores than for herbivores?
cards.back: Animal tissue is easier to digest than plant cell walls, so less of what a carnivore eats leaves as feces.
cards.quote: assimilation efficiency tends to be higher for carnivores, because animal tissue is easier to digest than plant cell walls.
cards.section: Following energy through a consumer

cards.front: Why is net production efficiency low in birds and mammals compared with many invertebrates and fish?
cards.back: Birds and mammals respire most of what they assimilate, much of it to keep warm, leaving little for new tissue and offspring.
cards.quote: Net production efficiency tends to be low in birds and mammals, which respire most of what they assimilate, much of it to keep warm
cards.section: Following energy through a consumer

cards.front: A shrew and a predatory beetle each assimilate the same energy from the same prey. Which is likely to pass more production on to the next trophic level, and why?
cards.back: Likely the beetle. Net production efficiency tends to be low in birds and mammals, which respire much of what they assimilate to keep warm, and higher in many invertebrates.
cards.why: Same A, so P = A − R is larger where respiration is smaller.
cards.quote: Net production efficiency tends to be low in birds and mammals, which respire most of what they assimilate, much of it to keep warm
cards.section: Following energy through a consumer

cards.front: A herbivore population ingests 800 kJ m^-2 yr^-1, egests 200 and respires 450. Its food plants' production is 4,000 kJ m^-2 yr^-1. Find assimilation, production, the three efficiencies and the trophic transfer efficiency.
cards.quote: its respiration, R; and its production, P
cards.section: Following energy through a consumer

cards.front: In an illustrative one-year budget, herbivore production is 360 kJ m^-2 yr^-1. Predators ingest 200, egest 100 and respire 60. Find predator production and the predator link's transfer efficiency.
cards.section: Following energy through a consumer

cards.front: Illustrative closed budget (kJ m^-2 yr^-1): GPP 12,000, NPP 6,000. Herbivores ingest 1,800, egest 1,080, produce 360. Predators eat 200, egest 100, produce 40, respire 60. Decomposers respire 3,240. How much detritus is stored, and does it reconcile with NEP?
cards.back: Detritus inputs: 4,200 + 1,080 + 160 + 100 = 5,540; minus 3,240 respired = 2,300 stored. Total respiration 6,000 + 360 + 60 + 3,240 = 9,660, so NEP = 2,340 = 2,300 detritus + 40 predator production.
cards.why: Unconsumed production enters detritus; GPP = Reco + NEP in a closed system.
cards.quote: NEP = 12,000 − 9,660 = 2,340, which is the 2,300 of detritus plus the 40 of predator production.
cards.section: Following energy through a consumer

cards.front: In the illustrative grassland energy budget, who respired more: decomposers, or herbivores and predators combined? What does that say about where NPP goes?
cards.back: Decomposers respired 3,240 kJ m^-2 yr^-1 against 420 for herbivores and predators combined. Most NPP never passed through a grazer; it went through detritus.
cards.quote: Decomposers (bacteria, fungi and detritus feeders) respired 3,240, against 420 for the herbivores and predators combined
cards.section: Following energy through a consumer

cards.front: A student divides a fish stock (30 g m^-2) by the stock of their prey (10 g m^-2) on one summer day and reports a transfer efficiency of 300%. What is wrong?
cards.back: Stocks were compared. Transfer efficiency is a ratio of production rates in matched units and time; biomass carries no time unit, and fast-turnover prey can support a larger consumer stock.
cards.quote: Neither a ratio of biomasses (stocks carry no time unit) nor gross growth efficiency, P / I, is a transfer efficiency (Going deeper).
cards.section: Following energy through a consumer

cards.front: A consumer ingests 400 kJ m^-2 yr^-1, egests 160 and respires 180. Find its gross growth efficiency and its net production efficiency.
cards.back: A = 400 − 160 = 240; P = 240 − 180 = 60. Gross growth efficiency P/I = 60/400 = 15%. Net production efficiency P/A = 60/240 = 25%.
cards.why: Gross growth efficiency is a property of one consumer, not a transfer between levels.
cards.quote: Gross growth efficiency, P / I, is production over ingestion: a property of one consumer, not a transfer between levels.
cards.section: Gross growth efficiency

cards.front: Over one year, predators eat down a standing prey stock. Which of the three efficiencies can exceed 1, and which cannot?
cards.back: Consumption efficiency can exceed 1: they ingest more than the prey's production that year. Assimilation and net production efficiency cannot, since each is a share of what the consumer took in.
cards.quote: Consumption efficiency can: when consumers eat down a standing prey stock, they ingest more than the production below them.
cards.section: When a fraction exceeds 1

cards.front: Where does the '10% rule' for trophic transfer come from, and how should it be treated?
cards.back: A mean of about 10% derived from 48 published aquatic food-web models. It is a rough benchmark from aquatic models, not a law; real links vary widely.
cards.quote: a mean transfer efficiency of about 10%, the classic support for the 10% rule: a rough benchmark from aquatic models, not a law
cards.section: Detritus, transfer efficiency and the 10% rule

cards.front: What average energy transfer efficiency did a 2026 synthesis of 2,052 estimates find, and where was it highest and lowest?
cards.back: About 6%, highest in marine systems and lowest on land.
cards.quote: A 2026 synthesis of 2,052 estimates from 122 studies found a lower average energy transfer efficiency, about 6%
cards.section: Detritus, transfer efficiency and the 10% rule

cards.front: NPP is 50,000 kJ m^-2 yr^-1. Counting producers as level 1, what production reaches level 5 at 6% transfer per step, compared with 10% per step?
cards.back: Four transfers. At 6%: 50,000 × 0.06^4 ≈ 0.65 kJ m^-2 yr^-1. At 10%: 50,000 × 0.1^4 = 5. The 6% chain delivers about 13% of the 10% value.
cards.why: Small changes in efficiency matter once multiplied.
cards.quote: 0.06 × 0.06 × 0.06 = 0.000216, about 0.022% of NPP, roughly a fifth of what the 10% rule gives.
cards.section: Detritus, transfer efficiency and the 10% rule

cards.front: A study of 25 northern temperate lakes found that food-chain length increased with lake size but not with productivity. How does this bear on the idea that low transfer efficiency limits chain length?
cards.back: Length rose with lake size but not productivity, so energy shrinkage is one proposed limit, not the only one.
cards.quote: That fast shrinking is one likely reason food chains are short, though not the only proposed limit (Going deeper).
cards.section: Detritus, transfer efficiency and the 10% rule

cards.front: Algae in a lake are grown short of phosphorus but with plentiful carbon. Predict the effect on energy transfer from algae to grazing zooplankton.
cards.back: Transfer to herbivores may fall even though carbon (energy) is plentiful, because nutrient-poor producers are poorer food. Energy is not the only currency that matters.
cards.quote: Producers short of nitrogen or phosphorus may limit transfer to herbivores even when carbon is plentiful, so energy is not the only currency that matters.
cards.section: Food quality

cards.front: An ecosystem energy budget tracks only the grazing chain (plants, herbivores, predators) and leaves out detritus. What goes wrong?
cards.back: A large share of NPP can be missed. Production not eaten, plus feces, enters detritus, where decomposers respire much of it and the rest is stored, so the budget cannot balance GPP = Reco + NEP.
cards.quote: It assumes production not eaten during the period enters detritus (in real budgets some stays as living biomass, is eaten along another food-web link, or is exported).

cards.front: A light-and-dark-bottle study at one depth on one day gives GPP in mg O2 L^-1 h^-1. What else is needed to report the lake's annual production in carbon per square metre?
cards.back: A stated photosynthetic quotient (and respiratory quotient for respiration) to convert oxygen to carbon, plus replicated measurements through the water column and the seasons, with spread reported.
cards.quote: Converting them to carbon needs stated quotients: a photosynthetic quotient (moles of O2 released per mole of CO2 fixed) for production
cards.section: Design problem
